 | D46 | Literal/token/nonterminal/EOF symbol classification | **`LabProtocol.scala`'s `ProductionInfo.rhs` and `RuleFirstFollow.first`/`.follow` changed from `Vector[String]` (pre-rendered, backtick-quoted display text) to `Vector[RenderedSymbol]` (`{text, kind}`, `kind` one of `literal \| token \| nonterminal \| eof`), so the Lab's clients can style each symbol kind distinctly instead of inferring "is this a terminal" from surrounding backticks. The user chose the larger scope over a narrower client-side heuristic: implement the full structured kind distinction now (Scala core + protocol + client) rather than deferring it. A companion change — grouping the railroad diagram and FIRST/FOLLOW into one `<figure>` across Notebook/Paper/PDF, also requested at the larger scope in the same round — was tried and reverted; this decision (the symbol-kind classification itself) is unaffected and stands independently. `spec/lab-protocol-schema.json`/`site/src/lab/protocol.ts` regenerated to match; the JVM↔JS conformance gate (`check:lab-parity`) confirms parity under the new shape. Rejected: inferring kind client-side from text shape (fragile — a literal and a token can both be bare identifiers depending on the grammar) and adding `kind` to `GSym.Term` directly (the state-merging risk above). |
 | D47 | Sigil de-Yacc-ification: `%` → `name:`/`lang:`/`->`/`@` | **Settings-fence directives become YAML-style `key: value`: `%name X` → `name: X`, `%lang X` → `lang: X`. Token-line modifiers split by provenance: `%skip` → `-> skip` (ANTLR4's own `-> command` lexer-command syntax, borrowed verbatim — a bare `skip` names the one builtin command); `%external(pass)` → `-> <name>` (folds into the SAME arrow family: `->` followed by any identifier other than the literal word `skip` names a host post-lex pass, bare identifier, no parens); `%caseless` → `@caseless`; `%prec N` → `@prec(N)` (parens now, unlike the old two-word form). `%left`/`%right`/`%nonassoc` in `## Precedence` fences are explicitly UNCHANGED — real Bison syntax, out of scope.** | `%` is specifically a Yacc/Bison-ism that ANTLR4 doesn't share at all — ANTLR4 uses bare keyword blocks, `@`-action-blocks, `$`-references, and its own `-> command` lexer-command syntax — so keeping `%` project-wide bought no real ANTLR4 familiarity, only accidental Bison lineage. The redesign splits directives into "genuinely borrowed, matching real target syntax 1:1" (`-> skip` from ANTLR4; `%left`/`%right`/`%nonassoc` staying as real Bison syntax) versus "Gramaire's own invention, honestly marked as such" (`@caseless`, `@prec(N)`, `-> <name>` for external passes — this last one reuses the arrow container for a non-ANTLR4 concept, but was judged acceptable since Gramaire's own `.gram.md` files are never fed directly to real antlr4/bison anyway; full interop always goes through the IR/converters per D43's positioning). This avoids the "fake compatibility" trap of a sigil implying a semantic match that isn't real. |
 | D48 | Alternative delegate slot: `-> IDENT` / `-> IDENT(args...)` | **A rule alternative's trailing slot grows a sixth shape: `-> IDENT` delegates that alternative's action to a named implementation, instead of an inline `{% %}`/`{%? %}` action. `Alt` (Core AST) becomes a flat, epsilon-free six-alternative cross-product — `SymList Label Action \| SymList Label Delegate \| SymList Label \| SymList Action \| SymList Delegate \| SymList` — never a wrapper nonterminal with an empty alternative (same epsilon-free discipline as D27). A new reserved `ARROW` token (`"->"`) joins the Core's own lexis at the same level as `PLUS`/`STAR`/`LANGLE`/`RANGLE`/`COMMA`; confirmed zero collision risk empirically, since a bare `-`/`->` had no prior meaning anywhere in the notation's own vocabulary (an unquoted `-` was an "unexpected character" lex error before this). Extended in the same phase's direct follow-up with a parenthesized, comma-separated argument list — `Delegate : ARROW IDENT \| ARROW IDENT '(' ArgList ')'`, `ArgList : Arg \| ArgList ',' Arg` (left-recursive, matching the notation's own house style for comma lists, reusing the `COMMA` token already declared for macro-call `Args`), `Arg : IDENT \| TERM_LIT \| NUMBER` — enabling host commands like `-> channel(HIDDEN)`, `-> type(TOKEN_TYPE)`, or arbitrary custom ones like `-> my_custom(arg1, arg2, 42)`. A new reserved `NUMBER` token (`/[0-9]+/`) joins the lexis for the bare-number argument shape; the core `lr`-notation lexer had no numeric token class before this (not to be confused with `Tokens.scala`'s separate bespoke token-LINE parser, a different lexer). `Alt.delegate` changed from `Option[String]` to `Option[DelegateSpec]` (`case class DelegateSpec(name: String, args: Vector[String])`, `args` empty for the bare form) and `IRRule.delegate` from `Option[String]` to `Option[IRDelegate]` (mirroring exactly) — a breaking shape change to a field that had not shipped to any real-world consumer yet, so modifying rather than versioning it was judged acceptable. Each argument is carried through as its own literal source text (an identifier's name, a literal's unescaped content, or a number's digit string) — the IR never interprets it further. Mutually exclusive with an action by construction, not a runtime check (the grammar has no production combining both, so writing both is a parse error). Verified conflict-free under Canonical/LALR/IELR, including in `Gramaire.gram.md` (the full-notation meta-grammar), which already had its own `ARROW` token for `-> skip`/`-> pass` lexer-command modifiers and safely reuses it here since the two occur in disjoint rule contexts.** | Delegating an alternative's action to something named rather than inlined is the natural next step once actions exist as a slot at all (D3/D25) — a consumer application (or, in a later phase, a fenced implementation elsewhere in the same file) can supply the real implementation, without forcing every action into `{% %}` source text. Parameterization followed immediately once the bare form landed, since a real delegate target (a lexer channel, a token-type override, a custom host command) almost always needs at least one argument to be useful — deferring it would have meant re-deriving the same `Alt`/`IRRule` field-shape change a second time. Scoped narrowly this phase: only the syntax + IR field land; resolving the name (consumer-supplied lookup now, fenced-implementation lookup later) is explicitly deferred to the `## Externals` phase, which is a separate, later piece of work. Mirrors D42's predicate field precedent exactly for the IR-additive-field mechanics (encode/decode/validate/schema, goldens byte-unchanged when absent). |
 | D49 | `## Externals`: embedded fenced implementations for a `-> name` delegate | **A new OPTIONAL reserved H2, `## Externals` (ADR D29's "a nonterminal, or a reserved section" list gains a fifth member), holding one `### <name>` H3 subsection per delegate name, each with one or more real-language-tagged fences (` ```javascript `, ` ```rust `, …  — genuine host code, never a bare ` ```gramaire ` content-shape fence) providing that name's implementation body; one fence per target profile when an author embeds more than one. Canonical position: after the rule sections and the optional `## Precedence`, before the optional `## Error messages` and the always-present `## Generated tables` (`GramaireCheck.scala`'s `alwaysTail`/canonical-order check). A `-> name`/`-> name(args)` delegate (D48/D48-args) is now resolved, in order, by an embedded `### name` implementation here if present, else a consumer-supplied one at runtime (unchanged default). Purely additive: a grammar with zero `->` delegates needs no `## Externals` section, and a grammar with delegates doesn't have to define any of them here either. A `### name` with no fenced implementation inside it is a hard, located parse error (`Lr.parseWith`/`parse` themselves, not just an opt-in extractor); a `### name` defined but never referenced by any `-> name` is a warning, not an error (mirrors `unusedTokenWarnings`'s "warn on likely-unused, never hard-fail on merely unused" house style); the opposite shape — a `-> name` with no matching `### name` — is unchanged, unwarned, default behavior. `Grammar` gains `externals: Vector[GrammarExternal]` (`GrammarExternal(name, impl: Map[lang, code])`), populated the same way `Rule.doc` is (ADR D39): never by `Lr.parseWith`/`parse` themselves (so a self-hosted parse stays exactly equal to `Bootstrap.bootstrapGrammar`), only by the explicit `Lr.withExternals`/`parseWithDocs` opt-in. The IR gains a matching top-level, additive-when-non-empty `externals: Vector[IRExternal]` (`irVersion` stays 0) alongside `grammar`/`tables`/`conflicts` — document-level, not per-rule (unlike `delegate`, which lives on `IRRule`).** | The natural next step once D48/D48-args shipped the delegate *name* but deferred resolving it: an author who wants a grammar to be genuinely self-contained (no external wiring step) can now embed the implementation directly, while a consumer who'd rather supply it at runtime (a shared library of named handlers across many grammars, say) still can — the two resolution paths compose, they don't compete. Reusing `Rule.doc`'s exact opt-in-attachment shape (rather than baking `externals` into the self-hosted `lr` grammar itself) keeps this a bespoke document-structure/parsing concern layered on top of the notation, not a new core-grammar production — `Bootstrap.scala`'s actual productions, the self-host oracle, and the `Lr`-self-hosting goldens are all untouched, matching D29's "###+ is free presentational grouping" scoping (the `### name` subsections are validated by `Lr.parseWith` directly, not by the `##`-only structure gate). Mirrors D42/D48's additive-IR-field mechanics exactly (encode/decode/validate/schema, goldens byte-unchanged when absent). |
-| D50 | `gramaire lint --target <name>`: export-compat preflight | **A new CLI command, `gramaire lint --target <backend> <file>`, answering "will this grammar survive export to this backend, and if not, what specifically breaks?" — deliberately reusing the existing parse/IR-build/diagnostics pipeline (`Main.parseWithDocs` + `IR.buildIRP`, the same one `emit`/`check` already run) rather than a third, parallel compatibility model. `GramaireLint.gates(ir, backendName)` runs a small, first-version check set as `GramaireCheck.GateResult`s (mirroring `check`'s own structure/drift gate presentation, PASS/FAIL per gate with located `-` detail lines, non-zero exit on any finding — the same CI-scriptable convention `check` already uses): (1) **precedence loss** — confirmed empirically that `BackendAntlr.scala` never reads `ir.grammar.precedence` at all (ANTLR4 has no precedence-declaration syntax), while `BackendBison.scala` DOES consume it (D37/D38) — a non-empty `## Precedence` silently vanishes only on `--target antlr`; (2) **delegate loss** — confirmed empirically that NEITHER `BackendAntlr` nor `BackendBison` (nor any other first-party textual backend) reads `IRRule.delegate` (D48) at all: a `-> name` alternative renders as a bare actionless alt, the reference gone without even a comment; (3) **externals loss** — confirmed empirically that `IR.externals` (D49's embedded fenced implementations) is likewise read by no textual backend, so an author's embedded real-language code vanishes right along with the reference that names it. All three checks exempt the `ir` backend, which serializes the whole IR (delegate/externals included) as JSON and so loses nothing. Scoped deliberately narrow for a first version — three real, empirically-verified checks, not a speculative exhaustive compatibility auditor. Grown by a later follow-up phase to six checks, same shape, same restraint: (4) **alt-label loss** (`altLabelLoss`) — confirmed empirically that `BackendAntlr` never reads `IRRule.label` (D26) even though ANTLR4 has a genuine native `# Name` alt-label syntax it could target (checked for contrast: `BackendTs` DOES read `r.label` to prefer it over its own fallback name, so this is a real, backend-specific gap, not an inherent notation mismatch), while Bison/yacc has no alt-label concept at all — scoped to `antlr`/`bison` only, the two backends actually verified; (5) **predicate loss** (`predicateLoss`) — confirmed empirically that no first-party backend, `js` included (unlike delegate/externals, `IRRule.predicate`/D-predicates was never given a D51-style rendering), reads `IRRule.predicate` at all: a `{%? %}`-gated alternative exports as an unconditional bare alt, silently widening the accepted language rather than merely losing a decoration — exempt only `ir`.
